plan.contextChunk: This figure is a three-dimensional plot of a single space curve rendered in dark blue against labeled coordinate axes. The vertical z-axis is graduated with ticks and numerals at 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, and 12. The x-axis runs toward the lower left with ticks labeled 2 and 4 in front and -2 and -4 behind, and the y-axis runs toward the lower right with the same labeling, 2 and 4 on the near side and -2 and -4 on the far side. The curve spirals counterclockwise around the vertical axis while climbing steadily, completing roughly two full turns between the xy-plane and the top of the frame above z = 12; its circular cross-section has radius 4, so each loop sweeps out past the ticks marked 4 on both horizontal axes. Two arrowheads placed on the ascending curve show the direction of travel. Across the upper right, in bold, the formula r(t) = 4cost i + 4sint j + t k is printed. Holding the loop radius constant while the height grows in step with the parameter is precisely what produces the spring-like shape. The plot displays the graph of a vector-valued function whose circular motion in the horizontal plane combines with uniform vertical rise to trace a helix.

elements: vertical z-axis with arrowhead at top, tick marks and numerals at 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12
x-axis running toward lower-left with arrowhead, ticks labeled 2 and 4 on the near side and -2, -4 on the far side
y-axis running toward lower-right with arrowhead, ticks labeled 2 and 4 on the near side and -2, -4 on the far side
axis letter labels x, y, z at the arrow tips
the helix space curve r(t) = 4cos(t)i + 4sin(t)j + tk in dark blue, ~2 full turns rising from z=0 to z≈12.6
two arrowheads placed on the ascending curve indicating direction of increasing t
a moving marker point that travels along the curve (driven by slider/animation)
optional faint vertical drop-line from the moving point to the xy-plane and a faint radial line to the z-axis to expose radius and height
bold formula caption r(t) = 4cos t i + 4sin t j + t k in the upper-right region
live coordinate readout x=4cos(t), y=4sin(t), z=t near the moving point

interactions.label: Trace r(t)
interactions.teaches: Watching the point sweep a circle in the horizontal plane while climbing at constant speed makes the helix visibly the sum of circular (i,j) motion and linear (k) rise

interactions.label: t
interactions.teaches: Scrubbing t advances the point along the curve with live x=4cos(t), y=4sin(t), z=t, showing how the vector-valued function maps a single parameter to a 3D position

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: From above the helix collapses to a single radius-4 circle, confirming the horizontal motion is uniform circular; returning to 3D shows the same circle stretched upward into a spiral

interactions.label: Parametric curve
interactions.teaches: Editing any component reshapes the space curve and the moving point follows it, revealing which term controls radius, phase, and vertical pitch

demo_steps.title: Helix in 3D
demo_steps.narration: At t≈6.3 the point sits about halfway up the two-turn spiral. The horizontal distance from the z-axis stays 4 while the height equals t.

demo_steps.title: Top view = circle
demo_steps.narration: Looking straight down, every height projects onto one radius-4 circle — the i and j components alone give uniform circular motion.

demo_steps.title: Rise with t
demo_steps.narration: Back in 3D at the top of the range (t≈12.6), the point has completed two full loops; height grows in lock-step with the parameter.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World scale: x,y ∈ [-5,5], z ∈ [0,13]. Helix radius 4 in the xy-plane, z=t so two turns span t ∈ [0, 4π]≈[0,12.57]; sample the curve with ~400 points. Axes as thin black/grey lines with cone arrowheads; tick numerals grey. Curve dark blue #1f4e8c, line width ~2.5. Moving point a small sphere in orange #ff8800 for contrast; optional drop-line and radial guide in light grey dashed. Formula caption rendered as bold dark text overlay top-right. Camera standard isometric pose; 'Top view' switches to a top-down pose (elevation ~90°) so the helix reads as a circle. Keep the curve within radius ~4.2 so it sweeps just past the 4 ticks on both horizontal axes as in the source.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the helix as a THREE.Line from sampled points; on any equation_input change, re-sample all three components over the fixed t-domain and rebuild the buffer (catch parse errors inline and keep the last valid curve). The moving point, its drop-line, radial guide, and the live x/y/z readout all recompute from the current parsed functions at the current t. The traceHelix animation advances t each frame and writes back to the paramT slider so the two stay synchronized; pausing lets the slider take over. For the viewMode toggle, animate the camera between the isometric pose and a top-down pose rather than snapping, so the collapse-to-circle is itself instructive. Arrowheads on the curve are small cones oriented along the tangent at two fixed t values.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Animation for tracing r(t): the learner plays the motion, a point moves around the circle while rising at constant speed and leaves the helix behind, making the combination of circular horizontal motion and linear vertical motion visible.
- Slider for parameter t: the learner scrubs t, the point advances along the helix with live x=4cos(t), y=4sin(t), and z=t values, showing how the vector-valued function maps time to position.
- Toggle between top view and 3D view: the learner switches views, the helix collapses to a radius-4 circle from above and returns to a rising spiral in 3D, clarifying that constant radius and increasing height together form the helix.
- Equation input for the parametric curve: learner edits x(t), y(t), and z(t), pre-filled with 4*cos(t), 4*sin(t), and t; the helix redraws and the moving point follows the new curve over the same t interval.

authoredContext:
As mentioned, the name of the shape of the curve of the graph in the examplec. is a helix (the figure). The curve resembles a spring, with a circular cross-section looking down along the z-axis. It is possible for a helix to be elliptical in cross-section as well. For example, the vector-valued function r(t)=4costi+3sintj+tk describes an elliptical helix. The projection of this helix into the x,y-plane is an ellipse. Last, the arrows in the graph of this helix indicate the orientation of the curve as t progresses from 0 to 4π.

The graph of the third vector-valued function is a helix.

This figure is the graph of a helix in the 3 dimensional coordinate system. The curve represents the function r(t) = cost i + sint j + tk. The curve spirals in a circular path around the vertical z-axis and has the look of a spring. The arrows on the curve represent orientation.
